hints: Focus on what heating under reflux with excess acidified dichromate does to primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
Look at the IR of K for a strong sharp dip near 1700 cm-1 for C=O, and check if the broad O-H bands for an acid or alcohol are missing.
Use the need for a ketone product plus the branched-chain requirement for J to pick the secondary branched alcohol that oxidises to a branched ketone.
walkthrough:
**Classify the oxidation of J**

Think like a teacher first. Strong oxidation with excess $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{H}^+$ under reflux pushes the reaction to the end.

$$\text{primary alcohol} \rightarrow \text{aldehyde} \rightarrow \text{carboxylic acid}$$
$$\text{secondary alcohol} \rightarrow \text{ketone (stops there)}$$
$$\text{tertiary alcohol} \rightarrow \text{no reaction}$$

**Read the IR spectrum of K**

The spectrum shows a very strong, sharp absorption at about 1700 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. That is the classic $\text{C=O}$ stretch.

There is no broad absorption at 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for an alcohol O-H, and no very broad absorption at 2500-3300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for a carboxylic acid O-H. So K is not an acid and not an alcohol.

**Decide aldehyde vs ketone**

Both aldehydes and ketones contain $\text{C=O}$. An aldehyde also shows two weak $\text{C-H}$ absorptions around 2720 and 2820 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, and more importantly an aldehyde would not survive in good yield under reflux with excess oxidant, it would oxidise on to the acid.

Since K is formed in good yield with no acid O-H in the IR, K is most consistent with a ketone. Therefore J must be a secondary alcohol.

**Apply the branched-chain clue**

J is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$ and branched-chain. A secondary branched $\text{C}_5$ alcohol that gives a branched ketone is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$ oxidised to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COCH}_3$.

options.A: J is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, a primary branched alcohol. Under reflux with excess oxidant it would go all the way to the carboxylic acid, not stop in good yield at the aldehyde $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. Aldehydes are only isolated by distillation, not reflux.
options.B: K is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a ketone which fits the IR, and J is secondary. However J is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (pentan-3-ol) which is a straight chain, not branched-chain, so it fails the stated condition for J.
options.C: J is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3$, a branched secondary alcohol. Oxidation gives the branched ketone $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{COCH}_3$. This explains the strong C=O at ~1700 cm-1 with no broad O-H for an acid or alcohol, and survival in good yield under vigorous conditions.
options.D: J is primary branched, so vigorous oxidation would indeed give the acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. A carboxylic acid must show C=O plus a very broad O-H stretch from 2500-3300 cm-1. That broad band is absent in the spectrum, so K cannot be an acid.
